# @visio/image-optimizer design

Build-time responsive images. A source photo in, a `<picture>`'s worth of encoded variants out, with a `sizes` attribute the styling tokens compute so the browser downloads the candidate the fluid layout will render.

## Goals

1. One import gives everything an `<img>` needs: `srcset` per format, dimensions, a placeholder.
2. No runtime image service. Every variant is a static asset with a content hash, cacheable forever.
3. `sizes` is derived, not guessed. The layout already says how wide an image is in design px; the same value produces the attribute.
4. Same shape as the font optimizer: a pure library, a thin Vite plugin, content-addressed cache.
5. One small image dependency. Bun's own `Bun.Image` decodes, resizes and encodes photos, so there is no native binary. The one other dependency is resvg's WASM build, which draws the site's icon artwork ("Icons" below).

## Pipeline

```
photo.jpg?responsive ──resolveId──► absolute path + query
                          │
                        load ──► optimizeImage() ──► variants (width × format), placeholder
                          │            │
                          │            └── Bun.Image: EXIF rotate → resize → encode, on Bun's worker threads
                          │                cache: sha256(source hash + params + Bun version + CACHE_VERSION)
                          └── module: `export default { src, srcset, sources, width, height, aspectRatio, widths, placeholder }`
                                build: import.meta.ROLLUP_FILE_URL_<ref> per variant (emitFile)
                                dev:   /@visio/images/<name> served from memory
```

- **`src/index.ts`**: `<Image>`, `remoteImage()`, and the types an app and `@visio/sanity` use. The library functions are internal; the tests import them from `src/`. The one exception is the `./internal/select` entry (`src/select.ts`): `@visio/sanity` imports `selectWidths` from it, so a Sanity image gets the widths its `sizes` can pick, as a local image does.
- **`src/optimize.ts`**: `optimizeImage(bytes, { cacheDir, name, widths, placeholder })`. `widths` and `placeholder` are for the tests; the plugin passes the default widths, or those `sizes` selects. The quality is fixed: WebP 80, JPEG 85, PNG lossless. A width above the source becomes the source's own width, never an upscale, so the largest file is always as sharp as the source allows. Every width is encoded twice: WebP for the `<source>`, and the source's own container (jpeg, png, or webp) for the `<img>` fallback, so a PNG with alpha stays a PNG. A WebP source is encoded once and has no `<source>`. Variant names are `<name>-<hash8>-<width>w.<ext>`; the bundler adds its own hash on top. An encode in progress is shared by cache key: two modules that import one file with different `sizes` load at the same time, and the second waits for the first's common widths instead of encoding them again.
- **`src/encode.ts`**: `Bun.Image`, with the `bun` backend, so macOS writes the same bytes as Linux and one source has one cache entry on every machine. A pipeline runs on Bun's worker threads, so every variant of an image encodes at once and the dev server keeps answering while it does. libjpeg-turbo, libspng and libwebp keep the ICC profile and drop EXIF and XMP, so a Display P3 photo keeps its colours and a phone photo's GPS never ships. The resize rounds the height down, so a 160px variant of a 3:2 photo is 106px tall; the module records the real size of each file. The placeholder is a WebP at most 16px on its long side (quality 60) inside an SVG with a Gaussian blur, drawn stretched to the box, as a URL-encoded `data:image/svg+xml,` URI with only `<`, `>`, `#`, `"` and `%` escaped. On the test fixtures it is 380 bytes for the photo and 511 for the PNG with alpha. The placeholder is the one exception to the metadata policy: the code takes the `ICCP` chunk out of its WebP, because `Bun.Image` has no option to drop it. A blur needs no exact colour, and a Display P3 profile would add about 500 bytes to every inline placeholder. `Bun.Image` has a ThumbHash placeholder of its own; on the lab's images it was larger, a plain gradient on the portrait, and smeared on the logo with alpha. The file types the part of `Bun.Image` it uses, because the Bun types in an app's tsconfig would let browser code use `Bun` too. Under Node it stops with an error that names the fix, `bun --bun vite`.
- **`src/cache.ts`**: the same shape as the font optimizer's. Keyed by the source's sha256, the encode parameters, the Bun version, and `CACHE_VERSION`, so a Bun upgrade (its codecs) or a change to the encode settings re-encodes. A file is written under a temporary name and renamed, so an interrupted build never leaves a truncated entry; a write that fails is a warning, not a failed import. The source is hashed once per image; each key is a hash of those short strings. After the last environment, a build logs how many variants came from the cache and how many it encoded, and deletes every cache entry it did not read or write, all of them when it loaded no image, so a changed image or a Bun upgrade does not leave its old files in the cache, and in Vercel's build cache, for good. Temporary files stay: they can be another process's write in progress. The dev server never deletes.
- **`src/vite.ts`**: `images()` and `svg()`, the public plugins. They take no options (see "No options" below). `src/images-vite.ts` is the images plugin. It claims `*.{jpg,jpeg,png,webp}?responsive` and leaves `*.svg?responsive` to the svg plugin; `?responsive` on any other file is an error. It resolves the file through Vite so relative imports and aliases work, and emits one const per variant so the `srcset` templates read plainly in the generated module. The client build emits the assets and lets the bundler resolve their urls; a server build, which runs after it, receives the final client file names as plain strings, so server-rendered markup points at the client assets rather than at files inside `dist/server`. The plugin is shared by both builds and keeps the client's result per module id without the bytes, so the server build's `load` is a lookup; in dev, or for a server build on its own, it takes the full path.
- **`src/vite-assets.ts`**: the glue both plugins share: the dev middleware that serves files from memory, and the URL of a file in dev, in the client build, and in the server build. Output names keep only `[\w-]` from the source name, so a space or a comma never reaches a `srcset` or a dev URL. In dev, a module that loads again replaces the files it registered before.

## Why WebP and no AVIF

The optimizer once wrote AVIF too, and gave it the first `<source>`. On the site's photos AVIF was 0 to 40% smaller than WebP, while WebP is already 4 to 8 times smaller than the JPEG. The cost was the encode: AVIF at effort 4 took 93 s for one 3840px variant of the lab's `wide.jpg`, and 172 s for all its variants, against 4.3 s for WebP and JPEG. Because wasm-vips, the encoder then, encoded on the event loop, a cold dev server answered no request while it encoded: the lab's first smoke run timed out after 3 minutes, and Vite's module runner stopped waiting after 60 s. Every browser the site supports decodes WebP. So the format list is not an option: an option that makes a cold start take minutes is a trap that no check reports.

## No options

`images()` and `svg()` take no options. The widths, the quality, the placeholder, the highest pixel ratio and SVGO's settings are fixed. An agent that sets a lower quality or a shorter width list makes every image worse, and no check reports it. The plugins have no parameter, so an option given to one is a type error. The tests set the widths, the placeholder and SVGO plugins through the internal modules in `src/`.

## The `sizes` attribute

`sizes()` lives in `@visio/styling` (`src/sizes.ts`) because it is a function of the tokens, not of the image. The styling compiler replaces each call with the string it evaluates to, the way it compiles `css()`; nothing about it runs in the browser, so a component whose tokens import is dropped once `css()` is compiled away still gets the right value. It takes the values authors already write, `dp(n)`, `columns(n)`, `t.layout.col`, or a design px number, per screen or once for both, and reads the design number back out of the string templates.

Below the desktop breakpoint `--frame` is `100vw`, so a design width of `w` px on a `d` px design is `w / d * 100vw`. Above it `--frame` is `min(100vw, maxWidth)`, so the same share is capped at `w * maxWidth / d` px. The clauses start at the widest screen, each with `(min-width: from)`, the same breakpoint as the stylesheet's `@media (width >= from)`. The narrowest screen is the last value, with no condition. A `(max-width: from - 1)` clause would leave a gap: at a viewport of 799.5px, which zoom can give, no clause matches it and the browser takes the desktop value. The result for a full-width hero on the site's tokens:

```
sizes({ mobile: columns(4), desktop: columns(12) })
// (min-width: 800px) min(97.78vw, 1232px), 91.47vw
```

That is exactly what the CSS resolves the element to, so the browser's candidate choice matches the rendered size instead of defaulting to `100vw` and fetching the largest.

## `<Image>`

`<Image>` is the one component that renders what the plugin encodes. It takes a `?responsive` import or an `ImageSource` from a CDN (`sanityImage()` from `@visio/sanity`), and renders a `<picture>` with one `<source>` per modern format and the original as the `<img>`. The blurred placeholder is the `<img>`'s background until the chosen file decodes. `fit` is `cover` or `contain`, `preload` makes it the eager, high-priority image, `loading="eager"` loads it at once at normal priority (a slide hidden now and shown soon; every other image is lazy), and `imgRef` hands the `<img>` to a project's WebGL texture, so it uploads the file the browser picked. `crossorigin` is the `<img>` attribute, for that texture: it has to be in the server HTML, because the browser starts the download before hydration, and a request made without CORS cannot be read by WebGL.

Until 2026-10-07 the component was the site's `src/ui/Image.tsx`, and the lab kept a copy that had to stay identical by hand. It is in the package now, so every app renders the same markup. The component has no styles of its own. Its defaults are in the reset of `@visio/styling`, the lowest layer, so any class of the site wins: the `<picture>` fills its box (`height: 100%`), the `<img>` fills the `<picture>` with `object-fit: cover`, and `data-fit="contain"` switches the image and its placeholder to `contain`. The only inline style is the placeholder, which depends on the image's data. `class` goes on the `<picture>`, the box a site sizes. The lint rule `no-raw-img` has no exemption: an app never writes the `<picture>` itself.

### A URL the build does not see

A site shows images it does not own: a video's poster from YouTube, the media of a feed a worker fetches. Until 2026-10-10 `<Image>` took only a `?responsive` import or a CDN source, and the lint rule `no-raw-img` bans the `<img>`, so a project built a fake `ResponsiveImage` by hand, with an empty `srcset` and a width and height made up to carry the ratio. `remoteImage(url, { aspectRatio })` returns that value, typed `RemoteImage`: one file, like a `VectorImage`, so `<Image>` takes it without `sizes`, and lazy loading, `preload`, `fit` and `class` work the same. There is no placeholder and no `srcset`, because nothing encoded the file. The ratio becomes `width` and `height` on 1000 px of height, which the `<img>` needs only for its shape before the file loads. Without a ratio the `<img>` has no `width` and `height`, and a class on the `<Image>` gives the box its shape; the reset makes the `<img>` fill it. A ratio that is not above 0 throws.

## A box whose height decides the width

`sizes` can only describe a width. A box that limits the image by its height, a photo viewer with `fit="contain"` or a full-screen box with `cover`, shows the image at the height times its ratio, capped by the box's width for `contain` and raised for `cover`. A portrait photo in a full-screen viewer at 1235 px and 2x fetched the 2560 px file for 570 CSS px (2026-11-04, the issue #405). The ratio is per image and the height is per box, so neither side can write the attribute alone: `sizes(width, { height })` compiles each entry to `width / height`, and `<Image>` (`src/fit.ts`) turns it into `min(width, calc(height * ratio))` for `contain` and `max(...)` for `cover`, with the image's own `width` and `height`, before it reaches the `<source>`s, the `<img>` and a CDN source. Chrome 156 picks the expected file for `min()` and `max()` with `vw`, `px`, `vh`, `svh` and `dvh` inside `calc()` (checked 2026-11-04 in headless Chrome); Safari is not checked. A browser that cannot read an entry drops it and falls back to the next one or to `100vw`: a larger file, never a broken image.

In dev, `<Image>` checks each image once after it loads (`src/check.ts`). With `w` descriptors the `<img>`'s `naturalWidth` is the file's width over the density the browser chose, which is the width `sizes` gives, in CSS px, even when Chrome serves the image from a larger copy it already holds. The check compares that width with the width the image shows (the box and the ratio, by `fit`), and warns when the two pick different files in the `srcset` and differ by more than 1.5 times. It does not judge the file the browser fetched, because a cached larger copy would blame a `sizes` that is right. The message names the height when the box's height decides the width, and the width per screen otherwise. An agent cannot see from the code when a box needs `height`; the smoke run shows the warning on the page that does. It reads the box at load only, and skips a box 0 px wide or high, such as a closed panel, so a box that resizes later is not checked again.

## Width selection from `sizes`

The default widths are written for the largest image on the site. A thumbnail rendered at 90px never needs a 3840px variant, yet without more information every import gets every width, in two formats. The `sizes` attribute is the missing information, and the styling compiler is the one place that knows it per element: it evaluates `sizes()` to its string, and it sees `import photo from './photo.jpg?responsive'` in the same file. So when a `?responsive` import's value lands on an element with a static `sizes` (an `<img>`, a `<source>`, or `<Image>`), the compiler appends `&sizes=<attribute>` to the specifier, one parameter per distinct value. The image plugin reads them in `load` and hands `optimizeImage()` only the widths the browser can pick (`src/select.ts`, with the parser in `src/sizes.ts`).

The rule is the browser's own: it fetches the smallest candidate at least as wide as the rendered width times the device pixel ratio, or the largest when none is. Across viewports from 320px to 3840px and pixel ratios from 1 to 3, that leaves the candidates between the smallest rendered width and the largest times 3, plus the first one above, which is what a 3x phone asks for at the top of the range. When a candidate is exactly the largest need, it covers that need, and the one above is left out. A one-column image on the site's tokens keeps only the 640 variant; the capped hero keeps every width, because a 1232px box at 3x really does ask for 3696px. An entry of `sizes(width, { height })` is `width / height`, and the widths it can pick depend on the image's ratio and the screen height, which the build does not see, so it keeps every width. Only the readable subset of `sizes` is parsed, the shapes `sizes()` writes plus plain `dp` and `px` values and `min()` of them; anything else keeps every width with a warning. An import whose `sizes` is a prop, or that is passed to a component rather than rendered, carries no parameter and keeps every width, so an unknown value never loses a candidate. The styling compiler reports such an import as `RESPONSIVE_NEEDS_SIZES`, so the extra widths are a decision, not an accident.

The module id includes the query, so the same file imported with two different `sizes` is two modules; identical variants dedupe in the bundle by content.

## SVG

Vector files take a different road: nothing to resize, and the logos and icons of a site want to be inline so CSS can colour them and the page paints them without a second request. `src/svg.ts` is the library, `src/svg-vite.ts` the plugin (`svg()` from `@visio/image-optimizer/internal/vite`).

```
logo.svg?component ──resolveId──► <path>.svg.tsx?component
                          │
                        load ──► optimizeSvg() ──► JSX: export default (props) => <svg …file attrs… {...props}>…</svg>
                          │                            └── the Solid plugin compiles it by the .tsx extension
                          └── the .svg file is the module's watch file; an edit invalidates the component
logo.svg / logo.svg?url ──load──► optimizeSvg() ──► export default "<url>"
                                                    build: a hashed client asset, the server build gets its final name
                                                    dev:   /@visio/svg/<name>-<hash>.svg from memory
logo.svg?responsive ──load──► the same file ──► export default { src: "<url>", srcset: '', width, height, … }
filters.svg?defs ──resolveId──► <path>.svg.tsx?defs ──load──► optimizeDefs() ──► JSX: export default () => <svg aria-hidden … width="0" height="0">…defs…</svg>
```

- **SVGO 4** with its default preset, then three of our own: `prefixIds` seeded from the file's path, so two inline SVGs on one page cannot capture each other's `<pattern>` or gradient; a size when the file has neither `width` nor `height`: the viewBox pixels for the file, and for the component one line of text (`height="1em"`, the width from the aspect ratio), so an unstyled mark sits next to text at its size and not at the width of its container while the stylesheet is on its way, whatever units the design tool exported (a `viewBox` 702 wide is still `1em` tall); and an authored size is kept. The colours are the file's own: a one-colour mark has `currentColor` in the file. Until 2026-10-09, `?component&mono` rewrote every painted colour to `currentColor`. Every import had to remember the flag (a wordmark imported in two files needed it twice), it compiled a second copy of the file with ids of its own, and a shape with no `fill` stayed black. One edit to the file does the same for every import, so `&mono` is now an error that says to make it. The preset removes `href` from `<a>`, because SVGO knows only `xlink:href` there; a plugin before the preset saves it and one after the preset puts it back, so a link in an SVG still works. The SVGO settings are fixed; the tests add a plugin to count the passes.
- **JSX from the AST**, not from the string: the last plugin captures SVGO's tree and the emitter writes one JSX element per node, attribute values and text as string literals, so nothing in a file can read as code. Whitespace-only text is dropped, except inside `<text>`, `<tspan>`, `<textPath>` and `<a>`, where it is the space between words. The file's attributes come first and `{...props}` last, so `class`, `width` or `aria-label` from the call site win. Solid compiles the result to a template on the client and markup on the server; the ids are the same on both sides, so hydration meets what it expects. The emitter drops `xmlns` from `<svg>` elements, which is what SVGO's `removeXMLNS` does: inline, the tag name gives the namespace, and through the spread the attribute would only be set again at runtime. The `?url` file keeps it for an `<img>`.
- **Ids are per file, not per render.** One component rendered twice puts the same ids on the page twice, and `url(#…)` resolves to the first. Both copies are the same drawing, so this is harmless until the first copy has `display: none`: then the second loses its gradients and patterns too. Hide that copy with `visibility: hidden` instead.
- **One SVGO pass per file**: the plugin keeps SVGO's result (a promise, so two loads at once share it) per file, checked against the file's mtime with one `stat`, so the client and server environments and a plain import next to a `?component` one share it. `hotUpdate` drops the entry for a changed file.
- **A drawing is `?responsive`**: a large SVG an `<img>` loads on its own goes through `<Image>` like any other image, so it is lazy, decodes off the main thread and has its size before it loads. The module is a `ResponsiveImage` with one file: the `src`, an empty `srcset` and no `<source>`, the size from the file's `width` and `height` in px or else its viewBox, and no placeholder. A file with neither stops the build. The type is `VectorImage`, and `<Image>` takes it without `sizes`, because one file serves every width; the styling compiler leaves its import alone for the same reason. Until 2026-10-09 the lint rule `no-raw-img` let an `<img>` through when its `src` was a plain `.svg` import of the same file. A drawing passed as a prop or picked from a list failed it, and a project wrapped each drawing in a component of its own to get past. The rule has no exemption now.
- **Defs for CSS are `?defs`**: a filter, gradient or mask that CSS references with `url(#id)` is in no drawing, so nothing in its own file references it. `?component` would lose it twice: the preset's `removeHiddenElems` and `cleanupIds` drop an element that nothing in the file uses, and `prefixIds` gives a hash of the path to the id, so a CSS reference would break with no warning when the file moves. `optimizeDefs()` runs the preset with those two plugins off and without `prefixIds`, so the ids stay as written. The component takes no props and renders the defs in a root that is 0 by 0, `aria-hidden`, and `position: absolute`, so it is out of the layout and the accessibility tree. The root stays rendered, not `display: none`. In Chrome (headless shell 1243) the filter applies from a `display: none` SVG too, but Firefox and Safari are not checked. Only a filter was checked in a browser, not a gradient or a mask. A file with no id under the root stops the build, because nothing could reference it (the component replaces the root, so an id on it does not count). Two `?defs` files with the same id give a warning, once per pair, because the page uses the first one it renders. A deleted or renamed file leaves the list; a file whose import is removed stays in it until a restart. A `?component` file that names a `?defs` id in an attribute (`filter="url(#no-white)"`) gets the prefix on that reference too, so the reference comes from CSS. A CSS `url()` to a filter in another file (`url(/filters.svg#id)`) is not an option: Chrome applies only a filter in the same document. The lint rule `no-inline-svg` names `?defs` when the pasted `<svg>` holds defs alone (`packages/oxlint-plugin`).
- **Types**: `*.svg?component` is `Component<JSX.SvgSVGAttributes<SVGSVGElement>>` in `client.d.ts`, `*.svg?defs` is a `Component` with no props, and `*.svg?responsive` is a `VectorImage`; a plain `.svg` import stays the string `vite/client` declares, for CSS or a meta tag.
- **Left to Vite**: `?raw`, `?inline`, and `url()` references from CSS, which Vite copies as they are.

## Icons

`src/icons.ts` (entry `./internal/icons`) converts the icon artwork of a site into the icon files. `visio()` owns the convention, the checks and the plugin (`packages/visio/DESIGN.md`, Icons). This package only converts, because it already holds `Bun.Image` and SVGO. `fillsCorners()` is the one reading: whether the drawing is opaque at its four corners, for visio's touch icon notice.

- **SVG to PNG with resvg.** `Bun.Image` does not decode SVG: in Bun 1.4.2 it stops with "unrecognised format (expected JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, TIFF, HEIC or AVIF)". So `rasterizeSvg()` uses `@resvg/resvg-wasm` 2.6.2: one package with no dependencies, 2.5 MB unpacked (a 2.4 MB `.wasm` file), with no native binary and no install script. The native `@resvg/resvg-js` is 4.4 MB for each platform, with a binary per platform as an optional dependency. The WASM build loads once for each process. It loads no system fonts, so a `<text>` element stops the conversion with a message: the PNG would lose the text, and the result would change from one machine to the next. An icon that is not square, or that links an image file, also stops it. `checkIconSvg()` runs the same checks without a PNG, for the dark variant.
- **The ICO by hand.** `encodeIco()` writes a 6-byte header, a 16-byte directory entry for each image, and then the PNG files as they are. Every browser, and Windows since Vista, reads PNG entries. The favicon has 16, 32 and 48 px.
- **A touch PNG** goes through `Bun.Image`: `resizePng()` makes it smaller, and stops when it is not square or smaller than the largest icon (512 px).
- **The dark variant.** `faviconSvg()` puts the light and the dark SVG into one file, each in a nested `<svg>`. A `<style>` shows one of them by `prefers-color-scheme`. SVGO prefixes the ids and classes of each file differently, because a `<style>` in an SVG applies to the whole file: without the prefix, a class of the dark file could paint the light drawing. One file needs one link. Chromium and Firefox apply the media query inside an SVG favicon. The `media` attribute on a second `<link rel="icon">` is not applied the same way in all browsers. A browser that does not show SVG favicons takes the ICO, which is the light drawing, or `icon-ico.svg` when the site has one (`visio/DESIGN.md`, Icons). Safari shows SVG favicons since Safari 26, but WebKit bug 309949 (March 2026, Safari 26.3) reports that it ignores `prefers-color-scheme` inside one, so Safari can show the light drawing on a dark tab. Not reproduced here. A mark that reads on a light and a dark tab avoids both cases; that is the designer's decision.

## Why Bun

Vite runs on Bun (`bun --bun vite`) so that the plugin can call `Bun.Image`; Vite has no Node API for it. The encoder before was wasm-vips: 13 MB of WASM, one encode at a time on the event loop, and on Bun every encode deadlocked. On the lab's `wide.jpg`, its 16 WebP and JPEG variants took 3.9 s with wasm-vips one after another, and 0.9 s with `Bun.Image` at once on 4 cores; the files are within 5% of each other in size. The tests run in `bun test` itself.

The test fixtures are noise, so the repo carries no third-party photos. They were made with libvips, and so were the site's sample images (`site/src/assets/images/dunes.jpg` and `studio.jpg`), by `test/make-fixtures.ts`, removed with wasm-vips; see git history. `p3-exif.jpg` is a Display P3 JPEG with EXIF and XMP, for the metadata policy. `rotated.jpg` is stored 300 × 200 with EXIF orientation 6.

## Not yet built

- Art direction: one source per screen. `sizes()` already speaks per screen; the module shape would need a `sources` list per input.
- Resized remote images. `remoteImage()` renders one file as it is; a URL from a CDN that resizes on request needs the CDN's own parameters, the way `sanityImage()` builds them.
- SVG sprites. One `<symbol>` sheet per page would save bytes on a page with many repeated icons; inline components are enough for a nav and a footer.
